narration:
Lanterns still burn by the coaching inn's door, though the sky to the east has already gone pewter. The wayside square is really just a wide patch of packed earth where three roads meet. There's a stone trough, a leaning signpost, and the notice board, which is papered so thickly the corners have curled into scrolls. Two carters argue quietly over a wheel. A boy sweeps horse dung toward the gutter with more energy than aim.

Beside the board stands a broad man in an oilcloth coat with a slate under his arm. He's chalking something out and crossing it through.

The nearest person is an old woman crouched over a brazier of chestnuts. She looks up at you, then at the compass at your belt, and her mouth twitches.

"Going on? Flood went down last week, that's what." She flicks a split chestnut onto the coals. "Took half the causeway markers with it, and the fen road's not where anybody remembers it being. Carts are stuck here waiting, as you can see. Tobin there," she says, nodding at the man with the slate, "has been posting work since sunup yesterday. Guides, diggers, folk to fetch strayed beasts." She squints at you. "Mostly he's been turning people away. He says too many of them can't tell north from their own backside."

Tobin glances over at the sound of his name. He takes in the stranger, rubs the chalk off his thumb, and waits.

arguments.value: Tobin's terms: strayed beasts 4 pennies/head alive, 2 dead w/ proof. Stone crew 1 silver/day, more for sighting lines. Convoy guide (6 wagons) 5 silver on arrival, nothing in advance. Test: leaning signpost reset by eye after flood. Truth: the fen-road arm is off by roughly a quarter turn (points too far west); the other two are near enough. A compass reading plus observation of the road ruts can show it.

narration:
Tobin hears you out without interrupting. His eyes go once to your hands, once to your boots, and once to the compass. Then he tucks the slate under his arm.

"Honest pay's what I've got. Honest hands are what I'm short of." He taps the board behind him, three notices in one blocky hand. "Strayed beasts. Four pennies a head brought back alive, two if it's dead and you can prove whose it was. Stone crew: a silver a day to dig the boundary stones back upright, and a bit more if you can sight a straight line between them. The digging's easy. Getting them where they belong is the hard part." He jerks his chin toward the carts. "And a guide for that lot. Six wagons across the fen causeway, five silver at the far end. I don't pay a penny before the far end."

One of the carters stops arguing long enough to listen.

"I'll be plain. I've had four 'guides' since yesterday. One of them walked a mule into a sump hole." Tobin rubs his thumb clean and looks at the signpost by the trough. It leans like a drunk, with three arms pointing roughly toward three roads. "That post went over in the flood. Gil set it back up by eye." He nods at it. "Tell me which arm's lying, and by how much, and we'll talk about the causeway. Can't do that? Then the beasts are still worth the walking."

Behind you the chestnut seller makes a small noise, as if she's settling in to watch.

narration:
Tobin doesn't smile, but some of the stiffness goes out of his shoulders. He pulls the slate from under his arm and turns it so you can read the chalk.

"Beasts, then. Good. Honest walking." He runs a thumb down the column. "Nine head that I know of. Four ewes from the Harrow flock, ear-notched twice on the left. Two nanny goats belonging to the inn. Three geese, and I'll pay for those, but I won't weep over them." He taps the last line. "And a brown mule with a white blaze and a split ear. That one's Dunne's."

The carter who had stopped arguing lifts his chin. He's a lean, sunburnt man, and he looks like he hasn't slept. "She'll come to her name. Hazel. She won't come to anyone who shouts at her."

"Last anybody saw of the sheep, they were on the fen edge west of here, out by the old peat cuttings, where the alder carr starts," Tobin goes on. "Goats will be wherever there's something to ruin. Four pennies a head brought here alive. Two for a dead one, if you bring the notched ear or something the owner can swear to. You get paid when they're standing in that pen behind the inn, not before."

"By when?" He looks east, where the sky is getting lighter. "Dusk tomorrow. After that the owners write them off, and the crows and the sumps take what's left." He chalks something new at the bottom of the slate. "Name?"

He writes ROWAN in blocky capitals. He doesn't cross it out.

"The post's still leaning," he adds, without looking at it, "if you get bored of goats."

narration:
Behind the coaching inn the road west narrows to a cart track between a wattle fence and a ditch full of brown water. The pen Tobin mentioned is here: hurdles lashed to posts, empty, the straw trodden flat. Beyond it the land drops away into the fen. It's a flat grey-green sheet under a paling sky, with dark lines of alder far off and pools lying everywhere like broken glass.

You walk slowly and watch the ground as much as the horizon.

narration:
The peat cuttings run in long straight trenches, as if somebody once ruled lines across the fen and then let the water fill them in. Black floodwater stands level with the brim. Between the trenches the turf baulks are barely a stride wide. Some are dry and furred with rushes. Others sit a hand's depth under the water, so you can only follow them by the faint ripple where the surface breaks over them.

The bleating is coming from out in the middle. Three dirty grey shapes huddle on a hummock where four baulks meet. It's an island of old turf no bigger than a cart bed. Water surrounds them on every side.

You don't go straight at it. You crouch at the edge and look for the baulks that carry rushes, because roots mean firm ground. You read the ripples and test each step with your heel before you put your weight on it. Where a baulk dips under the water, you find a fallen alder branch and probe ahead with it.

narration:
The walk back takes longer than the walk out. Your clothes are still heavy with peat water from the trench, and they're cold against your ribs. By the time the coaching inn's chimneys show over the wattle fence, your teeth have started to chatter. The pen behind the inn is as empty as you left it.

Tobin is at the board. He sees you coming, sees that nothing is following you, and doesn't put the slate down.

He listens to all of it: three ewes alive on the hummock, one of them stuck belly-deep on a drowned baulk off the island; the rotten baulk, third from the east edge; the dead one in the sump, which you found by touch and nothing else; a mule braying somewhere past the carr.

"Pen's empty," he says when you finish. He isn't unkind about it. "Slate says nothing owed." He taps the line with your name. "A dead one's two pennies when I've got the ear in my hand. Not when somebody tells me they felt it down there. You know where they are now. That's worth something to you. It isn't worth anything to me yet."

A stool scrapes behind you. Dunne is on his feet, and his tired face has gone sharp.

"Past the carr? Braying?" He's already pulling a coil of rope and a worn leather halter from under his cart's seat. "That's her. She'll be in the soft ground. She'll fight anything that pulls at her." He pushes both into your hands. "Go slow. Say her name low. Don't haul. Let her find her own feet."

Tobin glances east at the climbing sun, then at the drip running off your sleeve.

"Dusk tomorrow," he says. "Get dry first. A man shaking that hard drops things."
